title: Learning from the ‘Voyage of the Damned’: The Making of a Russian Naval Disaster
gist: Using engineering officer Eugene Politovsky's letters from the Russian Second Pacific Squadron's seven-month voyage to Tsushima in 1905, the author extracts five diagnostic indicators of a fleet that looks ready but is not: political interference in force design, inadequate training, poor material readiness, neglect of sailor welfare, and pervasive fatalism. He then maps each onto the modern US Navy, from congressionally mandated ship retentions and run-down maintenance infrastructure to fires aboard USS Gerald R. Ford and the cancelled Constellation-class frigate.

insights.claim: Eugene Politovsky's letters from the Russian Baltic Fleet's 1904-1905 voyage yield five observable indicators that a force is unfit for battle: excessive political interference in operational decisions, inadequate training, poor material readiness, insufficient concern for sailor welfare, and a pervasive sense of fatalism.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: A reusable checklist for judging whether any modern navy's declared readiness is real, useful when assessing deterrence credibility in the Pacific or the Red Sea.
insights.locator: The volume reflects the racial and gender assumptions

insights.claim: Fleets can project readiness externally long after their underlying effectiveness has begun to erode, which is why the Russian squadron passed Singapore in apparently respectable order in April 1905 weeks before its destruction.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Visible order of battle and hull counts are weak proxies for combat power, so investors and analysts should weight training, maintenance and retention data over fleet size announcements.
insights.quote: fleets can project readiness externally long after their underlying effectiveness has begun to erode
insights.locator: That appearance of competence is central

insights.claim: Tsushima is better read as the final exposure of a long-developing fiction of readiness than as a sudden catastrophe, because the defeat was the culmination of political interference, shifting aims, weak logistics, inadequate training, poor material condition and disregard for sailor welfare.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Institutional decay accumulates quietly and is only priced at the moment of conflict, which is precisely when repositioning is impossible.
insights.quote: Tsushima was less a sudden catastrophe than the final exposure of a long-developing fiction of readiness
insights.locator: The failure of the Russian Second Pacific Squadron

insights.claim: Tsar Nicholas II overrode military judgment by rejecting Vice Admiral Rozhestvensky's preferred compact force built around the four new Borodino-class battleships, after officers returning from the destroyed Pacific Fleet persuaded him that numbers mattered more than readiness, adding old vessels capable of only five to eight knots.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Political preference for headline force size over capability is a recurring failure mode that converts a difficult mission into an unwinnable one before deployment begins.
insights.locator: Political Interference

insights.claim: The imperial government attached Admiral Nebogatov's even older coastal defense squadron after the main fleet had already sailed, forcing a wait in Madagascar and slowing the combined force when the ships joined in French Indochina on May 9, 1905, weeks before battle.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Mid-deployment force additions imposed for political reasons can destroy the speed and schedule advantages that made the original plan viable.
insights.locator: Matters worsened when the imperial government added

insights.claim: Rozhestvensky's dismissal of Nebogatov's reinforcement as "archaeological rot" was crude but not misplaced, since the older ships reduced fleet speed, delayed progress and complicated operational planning.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Commanders often diagnose forced-on capability correctly in private while being unable to refuse it, a signal to read leaked internal criticism as data.
insights.locator: Rozhestvensky's contempt for Nebogatov's command

insights.claim: Congressional insistence on keeping aged US warships in the fleet past their retirement point, and conversely dispatching too few aircraft carriers to strike Iran during Operation Epic Fury, are modern examples of setting force levels for political rather than operational ends.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Legislated hull retention inflates apparent fleet size while consuming the maintenance and manpower budget that produces actual availability.
insights.locator: Likewise, in the present, the insistence of the U.S. Congress

insights.claim: Sustained underfunding across multiple presidential administrations has cut deployable US carrier mass relative to earlier campaigns, when six carriers deployed for the 1991 Gulf War and five large flattops supported Operation Iraqi Freedom.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Carrier surge capacity is a measurable, declining metric that constrains how many simultaneous contingencies the United States can actually cover.
insights.locator: improved funding over multiple past presidential administrations

insights.claim: The Russian squadron conducted its first gunnery practice since departing home waters on Jan. 26, 1905, and Rozhestvensky judged the results "too shameful to be mentioned" after his ships failed in daylight to hit practice targets representing Japanese torpedo boats.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Live-fire frequency is a cheap, hard indicator of a navy's real combat proficiency and is often the first thing sacrificed to schedule.
insights.locator: Poor Training

insights.claim: As late as April 1905, one month before the decisive battle, the Russian squadron's crews were still not accustomed to general night alarms and remained unprepared for night combat.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Proficiency deficits do not self-correct with deployment time; without deliberate training, months at sea produce fatigue rather than skill.
insights.locator: Even in April 1905, only a month before battle

insights.claim: During a February 1905 wargame off Madagascar, Rozhestvensky's subordinate admirals playing the opposing red team got lost and could not even locate his blue force, forcing him to spend the rest of the training day teaching basic ship maneuvers.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Senior-leader tactical incompetence is a leading indicator of formation collapse under fire and is visible in exercise results long before combat.
insights.locator: Collisions between ships were common

insights.claim: At the opening of the Battle of Tsushima the Russian battle line mishandled a basic turning signal, throwing the formation into disorder and preventing some ships from bringing their full armament to bear.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: The decisive failure was an elementary peacetime skill, reinforcing that training shortfalls surface at the worst possible moment.
insights.locator: Most consequentially, at the opening of the Battle of Tsushima

insights.claim: The battleship Alexander III repeatedly filed inaccurate coal consumption reports, and one such error forced Rozhestvensky to abandon an attempted high-speed dash to Vladivostok by the squadron's newest ships.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Bad internal reporting destroyed the only remaining operational option, a reminder that data integrity is itself a combat capability.
insights.locator: Officer proficiency was no better

insights.claim: The Russian squadron's paper firepower slightly exceeded Japan's, with more than 32,000 pounds of broadside weight across 26 twelve-inch and 15 ten-inch guns against roughly 28,400 pounds for the Japanese, yet the better-handled Japanese force won decisively.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Quantified materiel superiority is not predictive of outcomes, which should temper capability-count comparisons of China's and America's fleets.
insights.locator: The danger of that illusion was reinforced

insights.claim: The US surface fleet's return to serious combat training through the Warfare Tactics Instructor program may have been key to its success in anti-missile and drone battles in the Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz, while navies that skipped it faltered, as with the Danish frigate Iver Huitfeldt's inability to engage missile and drone threats and the Royal Navy lacking software to fire HMS Diamond's 4.5-inch gun at drones.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Combat-system software integration and tactical training, not hull numbers, separate navies that can shoot down drones from those that cannot, which favors suppliers of fire-control software and counter-UAS integration.
insights.locator: The U.S. Navy surface fleet neglected the kind of training

insights.claim: The post-1991 "long lee calm" degraded training across many Western navies, and only the return of sustained anti-missile and drone combat in the Middle East has forced them to rediscover continuous combat training.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Three decades of peacetime habits mean allied naval readiness is being rebuilt from a low base, implying multi-year demand for training, munitions and sustainment rather than new platforms alone.
insights.locator: The "long lee calm" of 1991 contributed

insights.claim: Even the Russian squadron's newest battleships were rushed into commission without sufficient trials to expose post-construction defects, and Politovsky, who had overseen aspects of Borodino's construction, worried that documenting those deficiencies would create enemies in St. Petersburg.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: When honest defect reporting is career-threatening, official readiness data becomes systematically optimistic, so external indicators matter more than declared status.
insights.locator: Poor Readiness

insights.claim: Auxiliaries meant to support the Russian fleet became liabilities instead: the repair ship Kamchatka generated more maintenance problems than it solved, the refrigerator ship Esperanza was detached after repeated breakdowns, and the transport Malay was sent back to Russia carrying medical and disciplinary cases.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Support and repair shipping is the hidden single point of failure in long deployments, an argument for investing in tenders and forward repair rather than only combatants.
insights.locator: Several auxiliaries intended to support the force

insights.claim: Russian logistical support was centralized under a single contractor, Ginsburg Inc. of Odessa, which had little experience sustaining a force of that size without a forward base, producing declining food quality, scarce clothing replacements, slow repair parts and mail delayed for months.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Outsourced sustainment without organic forward infrastructure is a structural vulnerability, directly relevant to assessing contractor-dependent US logistics in the Pacific.
insights.locator: Crew Welfare

insights.claim: Once Port Arthur fell on January 5, 1905, Vladivostok became the only viable destination, and the poor fuel economy of the older Russian ships made alternative routes avoiding the Tsushima Strait impractical.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Logistics constraints eliminate strategic optionality, so fuel and range economics dictate where a fleet can be forced to fight.
insights.locator: Russian officers did consider alternative routes

insights.claim: The US Navy allowed its own maintenance infrastructure to run down and replaced it with commercial contractors, the same path the Russian Second Pacific Squadron was forced to take, and while the return to shore-based intermediate maintenance is welcome, the Pacific remains an away game with no ability to repair combat-damaged ships in forward areas.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Forward battle-damage repair is an unfunded gap in US Pacific posture, pointing to shipyard, tender and allied repair-hub capacity as strategic bottlenecks.
insights.locator: The U.S. Navy's return to shore-based intermediate maintenance

insights.claim: A recent spate of fires on multiple US Navy ships, including the new carrier USS Gerald R. Ford, suggests that keeping one-third of a fleet of fewer than 300 ships constantly deployed and sometimes in persistent combat is exceeding what people and hulls can absorb.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Even brand-new platforms break when pushed beyond maintenance schedules, so deployment tempo is a leading indicator of future availability shortfalls.
insights.locator: People and equipment have breaking points

themes.theme: Sailor welfare and morale as operational variables

insights.claim: The Russian Baltic Fleet's deployment, the longest then undertaken by a steam-driven squadron, used ships never designed for prolonged hot-weather service, with temperatures regularly above 100 degrees Fahrenheit and engineering spaces nearly uninhabitable.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Platform design assumptions about operating environment set hard limits on where a fleet can be sustained, a live question for ships built for one theater and used in another.
insights.locator: Although the early 20th century brought improvements

insights.claim: Politovsky's account indicates dozens of Russian sailors died during the voyage itself from accidents, heat injuries, alcohol abuse, poor food and what would now be called friendly-fire incidents, before any battle was fought.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Non-combat attrition during transit is a quantifiable readiness drain that rarely appears in force-comparison models.
insights.locator: Politovsky's account suggests that dozens of sailors died

insights.claim: Morale collapse became an operational factor in its own right: suicides occurred after the fleet left Madagascar, sailors appear to have consumed opium-contaminated cigarettes in Cam Ranh Bay, and Rozhestvensky reportedly intended to relinquish command upon reaching Vladivostok.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Psychological depletion, including at the top of the chain of command, precedes and predicts operational failure but is invisible to outside observers.
insights.locator: A Perfect Storm

insights.claim: Almost 5,000 Russian sailors died at Tsushima and the broader disaffection of Russian sailors helped fuel the revolutionary unrest that followed, showing that neglect of a force's welfare can become a regime-level political risk.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Military failure driven by institutional neglect can convert into domestic political instability, a second-order channel worth watching in any autocracy fighting a losing war.
insights.locator: In the Russian case, the human cost was immediate

insights.claim: For a volunteer force, aligning the sailor experience with civilian living standards is a retention requirement, and the now-cancelled Constellation-class frigate would have replaced standard berthing compartments holding 30 or more sailors with six-person berthing rooms.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Cancelling habitability upgrades saves acquisition dollars while raising long-run manpower cost, a trade-off that shows up later in recruiting and retention shortfalls.
insights.locator: The now canceled Constellation class frigate

insights.claim: Reports of food shortages aboard US Navy ships during Operation Epic Fury proved false, and US ships maintain cleanliness standards far beyond those of the early 20th century.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: A check against overreading historical analogies: modern US sustainment failures alleged in the press did not hold up on inspection.
insights.locator: Reports of food shortages on U.S. Navy ships

insights.claim: When missions appear disconnected from achievable strategic objectives, morale degrades and retention suffers, which is why port visits and temporary respite did nothing to restore Russian confidence absent a credible path to success.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Strategic ambiguity has a measurable personnel cost, making clarity of mission a readiness input rather than a communications nicety.
insights.locator: Finally, strategic ambiguity and prolonged hardship

insights.claim: Theodore Roosevelt drew the opposite lesson from Tsushima by sending the Great White Fleet on a peacetime world cruise to demonstrate that sustained global naval operations were possible under better conditions.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: Long deployments are not inherently corrosive; the variable is the supporting institutions, which is the actual investment target.
insights.locator: Theodore Roosevelt drew part of the opposite lesson

insights.claim: As contemporary fleets are asked to do more with fewer ships, tighter maintenance margins and uncertain strategic purposes, readiness should be treated as a condition to be sustained rather than a posture to be displayed.
insights.speaker: Steven Wills
insights.so_what: The investable implication is sustainment, training and maintenance capacity rather than headline platform programs.
insights.quote: readiness is not a posture to be displayed but a condition to be sustained
insights.locator: As contemporary fleets are asked to do more
